events.title: Miguel de Icaza announces Mono
events.summary: Ximian unveiled the [Mono] Project on July 9, 2001 — Miguel de Icaza's open-source .NET implementation, with details presented at O'Reilly OSCON later that month.
events.about: [Mono] enabled Xamarin mobile development and Unity's C# scripting on [macOS] and Linux. de Icaza also co-founded GNOME and Ximian — shaping open desktop and cross-platform .NET.

narrative.whyChosen: [Mono] made [Microsoft]'s managed runtime portable before .NET Core existed.
narrative.whyImportant: It kept C# viable for cross-platform mobile and game development.
narrative.problemSolved: .NET was Windows-only, blocking open-source and mobile adoption.

events.title: BitTorrent client first released
events.summary: Bram Cohen released the first BitTorrent client on July 2, 2001 — a [peer-to-peer] protocol that splits large files into swarms of cooperating downloaders.
events.about: BitTorrent inverted [client-server] bandwidth: every downloader also uploads pieces to peers. Linux ISOs, game patches, and legal media used it to survive traffic spikes without giant CDN bills. The protocol influenced how engineers think about distributed file transfer and content-addressed chunks.

narrative.whyChosen: BitTorrent pioneered swarm-based large-file distribution on the open internet.
narrative.whyImportant: It showed [peer-to-peer] protocols could scale downloads without centralized bandwidth.
narrative.problemSolved: Popular files overwhelmed single servers; users needed resilient ways to share multi-gigabyte archives.

events.title: Code Red worm targets IIS web servers
events.summary: The Code Red [worm] peaked on July 19, 2001 — exploiting a buffer overflow in [Microsoft] IIS to deface websites and launch DDoS attacks against the White House.
events.about: Code Red scanned the entire [IPv4] space for vulnerable IIS installs — hundreds of thousands of servers compromised in hours. It was named after Mountain Dew flavor at eEye Digital Security and forced emergency patching of Windows NT and 2000 web farms. Developers learned that internet-facing services could be weaponized into botnets overnight.

narrative.whyChosen: Code Red showed how one IIS bug could infect the public web in a single day.
narrative.whyImportant: It accelerated automated patching and incident-response teams for internet services.
narrative.problemSolved: Nothing initially — it exploited unpatched buffer overflows faster than admins could deploy fixes.
